Third, it contains a reference to the Spring of Life. And taken as a whole, its account of the twelve universes strikingly recalls the ancient theologies of Aiôn, or eternal cosmic time, with their twelve millennia. Here is the story as Jâbir tells it.

“I asked the Imam how to understand this verse of the Quran: ‘Thus We showed Abraham the Malakût of the heavens and the earth’ (6:75). I was sitting with my head lowered toward the ground. The Imam raised his hand and said to me: ‘Lift your head.’ I lifted my head and looked toward the ceiling. It had opened, and through the opening I could see a light so intense that it dazzled me. The Imam said: ‘That is how Abraham saw the Malakût of the heavens and the earth.’ Then he said: ‘Look toward the ground.’ I looked down. He said again: ‘Lift your head.’ I raised my head, and the ceiling was there once more.

“Then the Imam took me by the hand. We left the house where we had been sitting and entered another house. There the Imam took off the robe he was wearing and put on a different one. Then he said to me: ‘Lower your eyes.’ I lowered them. ‘Do not open your eyes,’ the Imam warned me. He let an hour pass, then asked: ‘Do you know where you are?’ ‘No, I do not.’ ‘You are in the Darkness through which Alexander traveled.’ I said to him: ‘May I be your ransom! Will you now allow me to open my eyes?’ ‘Open them. You will see nothing.’

“I opened my eyes, and indeed I found myself in a Darkness so complete that I could not even make out the ground beneath my feet. Then the Imam walked a few steps and stopped. He said: ‘Do you know where you are now?’ ‘No,’ I replied. ‘You are standing at the Spring of Life, from which Khezr drank. Drink this water.’ So I too drank. Then we left the world where we were and entered another world. We followed a road through it, and saw things whose forms resembled those of our own world: plants, dwellings, and inhabitants. Next we passed into a third world, which resembled the first and the second. Gradually we reached a fifth world.

“The Imam said to me: ‘All this is the Malakût of the Earth that Abraham did not see. He saw only the Malakût of the heavens. There are twelve universes like those you have seen. Whenever the time of one of us, the twelve Imams, is completed in the time of this earthly world, he dwells in one of these twelve worlds. This continues until the last of us, the Qâ'im—the twelfth Imam, the One Who Will Rise—comes into this universe in which we dwell with him.’ Then the Imam said to me: ‘Close your eyes.’

“I closed them. He took me by the hand, and suddenly we were back in the house from which we had set out. The Imam took off his robe and put on the one he had been wearing at the beginning. We returned to our original meeting place. I said to him: ‘May I be your ransom! How much time has passed?’ The Imam answered: ‘Three hours.’”

The exceptional interest of this account lies in its testimony to another actual entry into the Malakût, entirely comparable to the experience described in the story of the White Cloud. There would, of course, be much to say about the process and successive stages of this experience.

But the essential point is the organic connection, expressed through the number twelve, between our world and the Malakût, between the time of our world and the time of the Malakût. For these twelve universes are the very ones already described in the hadith of the Twelve Veils of Light (above, p. 148), with one difference: there they were presented in the order of their creation. That tradition told us that twelve Veils of Light were created either alongside the Muhammadan Light (Nûr muhammadî), first brought into being by the self-creating Will, or out of that Light itself. These twelve Veils of Light represent the respective universes of the twelve Imams, and they are also symbolized as twelve millennia.

During its descent toward its manifestation in the earthly world, in the person of the Seal of the Prophets, the Muhammadan Light dwells in each of these Veils. It spends twelve millennia in the first Veil, eleven in the second, and so on. From millennium to millennium it passes through the space of the Malakût, approaching the time of its earthly manifestation. Space has become time. Conversely, the twelve universes that the Imam shows Jâbir, now presented in the order of return, are the stages through which this Light rises again, from Imam to Imam, toward the “place” of its origin.

Time becomes space once more. Millennium after millennium, the time of its descent is folded back upon itself, returning the Light to the simultaneous fullness of the spiritual assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. It is this conception of twelve millennia that appears, within Shiite theosophy, as a remembrance of the Iranian-Hellenistic theologies of Aiôn. With Qâzî Sa'îd, we immediately understand that the Spring of Life lies in the first world of the Malakût, the first of the twelve worlds they enter. For this Spring of Life is the walâyat of the first Imam—his spiritual authority and the inner reality of his mission—and it is through knowledge of this walâyat that eternal life is brought into actuality.

But we should notice that the fifth Imam, Muhammad Bâqir, takes Jâbir into only five of these worlds of the Imams. The reason is simple. An earthly human being can enter the Malakût only through the form in which that Malakût has manifested itself in our visible world. At the time of Jâbir’s conversation with the fifth Imam, only five of the twelve Imams had appeared in this world. Jâbir can therefore enter only the Malakût belonging to the worlds of those first five Imams.

Still less could Abraham have entered the Malakût of any of the Twelve. This is entirely consistent with Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî’s metaphysics of time, in which time first expands and then folds back upon itself. With the twelfth Imam’s brief and fleeting appearance, the Malakût of the Perfect Human Being (Anthrôpos teleios) began to manifest itself. This is a complete universe embracing the Throne ('arsh), the celestial firmament (Korsî), the heavens, the earth, and everything that exists.

Yet its full manifestation in this world will occur only with the return of the twelfth Imam, the Resurrector. At that very moment, the folding of our chronological time into the subtle time of the Malakût will be complete. For it is only with the twelfth Imam that human reality attains the full stature of the Complete Human Being. The end of this brief digression brings us back to the traditional accounts of the cosmos assembled by our commentator, and particularly to the forty worlds mentioned by the Imam at the point we have reached in the story of the White Cloud.
We cannot hope to bring such varied indications into a single system. There is, for example, a hadith in which the same Jâbir reports hearing the fifth Imam declare:

“Beyond this sun of yours are forty suns, and between every two suns there are forty universes. In those universes live multitudes of creatures who do not know whether God created Adam or did not create him. Beyond this moon are forty moons, and between every two moons there are forty worlds. There too live countless creatures who are indifferent to, or ignorant of, whether God created Adam.”
In short, the traditional accounts concerning these pre-Adamic universes are innumerable. Gathering and organizing them would require a lengthy investigation.

We can, however, already identify one feature they share, especially those traditions that give the number forty in one form or another. They tell us that our Adamic world—the world of humanity as we know it—is not the result of what is nowadays called evolution, an evolution whose duration science even claims to calculate in the millions of years needed to pass from a single-celled organism to a human being! According to the thinkers we are studying, our Adamic world, and the human condition belonging to it, result instead from a descent through successive worlds.

Each of these worlds still lies beyond Mount Qâf, beyond the physical universe perceived by our senses and which our scientific instruments aspire to conquer. This descent continues until it reaches the present human world, which marks both the end of the descent and the beginning of the ascent. We are thus invited not to forget that every achievement accomplished by physical machinery remains, by definition, on this side of Mount Qâf.

Among the traditions cited by Qâzî Sa'îd, one that has exercised the ingenuity of many thinkers speaks of forty mornings during which the mysterious formation of a cosmic Adam took place. On each of these forty mornings, the sun of divine Emanation rose. There were also forty nights, on each of which stars appeared, each star a divine Light cast upon the human receptacle that necessarily took the form of the Light it received. The succession of these mornings and nights signifies the emergence of forty worlds of humanity.

But in relation to the one we call “Adam our father,” the humanity inhabiting these worlds was both pre-Adamic and of a higher order. This explains the references to forty Easts and forty Wests. Each new world is a West in relation to the world preceding it, which is itself the East of the world that follows. In each of these worlds, at every level of pre-Adamic humanity, a pledge was given in answer to the question recorded in the Quranic verse: “Alastu bi-rabbikum? Am I not your Lord?” (7:171). One master of mystical knowledge even affirmed that he had seen most of these worlds and retained their memory.
Another claimed to perceive the very vibration of the question and its answer as something taking place in his own time—in the particular measure of subtle time belonging to him, of course.

“There is a tremendous secret here,” Qâzî Sa'îd remarks in passing, “which you may come to know to the extent that you are able to cast off the garment of earthly human nature (nâsût) and rise to the horizon of the Malakût.”

And in each of these pre-Adamic worlds, the same rhythm of forty is repeated. That is why we heard the Imam declare that each world is equal to forty times our universe. Only at the end of this cosmic process of formation did the world and humanity of the “little Adam” (Adam al-saghîr) emerge: the Adam who is “our father.” As another hadith puts it, in words addressed by the fifth Imam to one of his close companions:
“God has created millions of universes and millions of Adams. You live in the last of these worlds and belong to the last of these Adamic humanities.”

What, then, are we to make of the narrowly bounded cosmos in which humanity was supposedly confined before the so-called modern age? But now, of course, we can understand why all these worlds lie “beyond Mount Qâf.” For Mount Qâf itself, the mountain with the emerald cities, is the Malakût of our own human reality, the spiritual world corresponding to the human condition that is ours. All this is implied in the Imam’s reply to Salmân the Pure at this moment in the story of the White Cloud.

And now the Imam—not simply the first among the Twelve, but the eternal Imam who represents the complete theophanic assembly of all Twelve—utters what sounds like a solemn psalm. Many sayings from the hadiths return within it as echoes and allusions. The twelve Imams appear as the complete assembly of the divine energies through which the cosmos comes into being. The visible phenomena of our world are their traces and manifestations.

“O Salmân! Our Names—the Names of the Imams—are written upon the nights, and so there is darkness. They are written upon the days, and so there is light. I am the ordeal that falls upon our enemies. I am the Great Upheaval (Quran 79:34). Our Names are written upon the Throne, and so it stands supported. They are written upon the heavens, and so they rise. They are written upon the earth, and so it stands still. They are written upon the winds, and so they whirl.

“Upon lightning, and so it flashes. Upon light, and so it streams forth. Upon thunder, and so it roars. Our Names are written upon the forehead of the angel Seraphiel, whose one wing extends to the East and the other to the West, and who proclaims: ‘Worthy of the highest praise, most holy is the Lord of the Angels and of the Spirit’” (§ 26).

These final words are like an echo of Yahweh Sabaoth, the Lord of Hosts, and of the threefold cry of holiness sung by the Seraphim in Isaiah’s vision—a vision that was also one of the sources of Kabbalistic metaphysics. Qâzî Sa'îd offers this interpretation:

“The Names here signify the Lights of the Imams rising from the realm of the Jabarût, the world of divine power. All beings of light receive their light from the first Light that emanated from the First Principle. That first Light is the Muhammadan Light, the Light of the complete assembly of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Everything that receives a share of this Light—which is being itself—receives it through the radiance of that primordial Light and the spiritual influx of that supreme Name.”

Earlier we learned that it was this cosmic, creative Imam who brought forth the angel entrusted with the darkness of the nights and the brightness of the days. This ordering and regulating activity does not occur without leaving something of its source within what it produces. That, Qâzî Sa'îd tells us, is what the “writing” of the Imams’ Names upon the nights, the days, and all the phenomena subsequently enumerated symbolically expresses. The idea that the structures and conditions of existence as a whole arise through the activity of the Imams, acting as a cosmic energy, is therefore gathered into a single image: their Names “inscribed upon the forehead of the angel Seraphiel.”

We encountered this angel at the very beginning of the story of the White Cloud. His forehead signifies the exalted metaphysical station of the twelve Imams. The East toward which one of Seraphiel’s wings extends signifies the rising place, the dawn of the lights of being (matla' anwâr al-wojûd). The West toward which his other wing extends signifies the world of matter in its material state, the world in which all beings of light live as exiles.

Thus the wing of Seraphiel that extends toward the East is the one through which he receives the influx from the higher worlds, while the wing extended toward the West is the one through which he pours that influx upon the lower worlds. Seraphiel thereby encompasses all beings that enter into the relationship of robûbîya, or divine Lordship. This relationship comes into being through the manifestation of the hidden God, the Absconditum. It makes the revealed God, the Deus revelatus, the Lord of beings through a reciprocal bond joining the Lord and the being over which he exercises Lordship.

The rabb, the Lord, and the marbûb, the one whose Lord he is, cannot exist in that relationship independently of one another. It would be unthinkable, however, for the Absconditum—the God beyond all description, of the theology that approaches God by negation—to enter into such a relationship. Hence Seraphiel’s cry of praise addressed to the one who is “the Lord of the Angels and of the Spirit.”

We now come to the dramatic episode that will bring the story of the White Cloud to its close. This episode offers a striking illustration of how our chronological time folds back into the subtle time of the Malakût. The particular kind of contemporaneity belonging to the Malakût allows visionary experience to witness events scattered throughout the past of our chronological history. This presupposes that the event taking place in chronological time presents us with only its outward face. Its true reality remains invisible and inaccessible to anyone incapable of entering the Malakût. There the companions will witness the destruction of the ancient Arabian people of 'Âd, who rebelled against the call of their prophet, as related in the Quran. Salmân the Pure resumes his account:

“Then the Imam said to us: ‘Close your eyes.’ We closed them. He said: ‘Now open your eyes.’ We opened them, and suddenly we found ourselves in a city larger than any we had ever seen. Its public places were crowded and bustling. Its inhabitants were taller than any human beings we had ever encountered. Each of them was like a palm tree.

“We asked: ‘Who are these people? We have never seen people of such extraordinary height.’ The Imam replied: ‘These are the people of 'Âd. They are unbelievers. They believe neither in the Last Day nor in the Prophet. ‘I wanted you to see them here, in this place of the Malakût, because in the lower world their time has passed. Their city, one of the great cities of the East, has been wiped away. ‘I have brought you here without your being aware of it. I wish to fight them before your eyes’” (§ 27).

Qâzî Sa'îd interrupts the narrative briefly to review several essential points of the metaphysics of time that we encountered at the beginning. The best course is to follow the central points of his commentary one by one.

Although their encounters with the prophet Sâlih and then with Solomon had already involved a folding back of time, our theosopher believes that what the companions had witnessed up to this point was primarily a transformation of our spatial world. What they now experience is a specific folding back of chronological time.

In other words, the Imam is initiating them into a vision of the Malakût of time itself, and of everything that exists in time (zamânîyât). The earlier episodes have already taught us what opening and closing the eyes means in spiritual initiation. Here, Qâzî Sa'îd explains, “closing their eyes means that the companions abandon their preoccupation with the Malakût of the Earth and the extraordinary things they have just witnessed there.” Opening them now means entering the Malakût of time, the horizon of everlasting duration (ufq al-dahr). Within that horizon, “all temporal things are like colored points threaded upon a string, or like shining pearls arranged along a necklace.
“Thus any being belonging to the Malakût (malakûtîyûn) can, whenever it wishes, choose whatever portion of time it desires.

“Earthly human beings, however, are confined within such narrow limits of perception that it would be useless to try to show them the whole. The Imam therefore shows his companions only a fragment of the Malakût of time.”
Everything we said at the beginning about Qâzî Sa'îd’s philosophy of time now finds its application in this final episode. Our author summarizes the question as follows:

“Understand that a being existing in time remains one and the same individual (shakhs wâhid) from the beginning of its existence until the moment when its visible presence comes to an end. It is a single, continuous reality. But because the particular measure that determines its form and appearance comes into view gradually, it appears to us in this world as something unstable, something that passes and flows away.

“Yet this in no way means that it is annihilated within the order of what actually exists, when we consider the thing as it truly is. Far from it! Such disappearance is impossible, for an individuality that constitutes a unity cannot both be annihilated and continue to exist. This decline and concealment are such only in relation to you, in relation to the imaginary representation (wahm) that dominates your intellect. Otherwise the person does indeed exist as one unified person (shakhs wahdânî), from eternity before time to eternity beyond time.”
There is also a common misunderstanding to guard against. None of this means that the whole of the past or the future is present within each fragmentary instant.

“I do not mean,” Qâzî Sa'îd clarifies, “that the totality of this unity constituted by a person exists within the present moment, the nunc. We cannot say that any more than we could say, when considering the extent of something in space, that the whole of that extent exists, for example, in its central portion. Nor do I say that past time exists within the things that, for you, have been left behind, or that future time exists within the things yet to come.

“For time is not itself something possessing a time and a place. To say otherwise would amount to speaking of a time belonging to future time, and a time belonging to past time. No. What I say is that the time which appears to you as the past, and the time which appears to you as the future still to come, are in fact embraced together (ta'ânaqâ) when seen from the supreme horizon. And they remain forever embraced for the one before whom there is neither morning nor evening.”

Qâzî Sa'îd then evokes the pages of the book that will be unfolded for every person on the Day of Resurrection. The pages are the successive days of a life, the individual’s measure of time on the scale of this world. The book is that life as a whole. And it is the entire book that corresponds to the Malakût of each person’s time. The pages that are turned do not disappear at all. A being of the Malakût can turn them backward or forward at will, and in the great Book of the world can even read pages that have not yet been reached. Our author then offers this comparison:

“Spend an hour beside a river, watching the water flow past. You would surely never imagine that the water which has passed beyond you has therefore ceased to exist. Well, it may be that for certain people whose hearts are pure, the course of time is like the course of the river.”

When the Imam shows his companions the city of the people of 'Âd, he is therefore showing these earthly human beings, temporarily transported into the Malakût, “a fragment of former places and former times.

“Each generation is like a city, because within it a group of beings is gathered, whose particular condition is to exist there. That the city belongs to the East means, in this instance, that it belongs to past times. For the past is the origin of chronological time, and that origin is indeed the East where the sun of the Lights and Spirits rises, before they begin their journey through the heavens of the present and the future. The unbelief of the people of 'Âd in the resurrection, and their rejection of the prophetic message, are two aspects of the same spiritual incapacity. For mystical theosophy ('irfân) holds that faith in the resurrection implies faith in the message of the Seal of the Prophets.”

In other words, so long as human reality has not attained the perfection represented by acceptance of the prophetic message, the return toward its origin—the ascent that folds time back upon itself—remains impossible.
“And this,” our commentator says, “is one of those doors that open a thousand other doors.”

Indeed, this opening allows us to see the connection between the spiritual reality of the Imam and the doctrine of the last things: between Imamology and eschatology. That is why, in numerous hadiths and sermons, the Imam declares:
“I am paradise and hell. I am the Great Ordeal, the Great Upheaval (al-Tâmma al-kubrâ).”

The return and manifestation of the Imam brings the folding back of time to completion. It produces the extraordinary contemporaneity experienced here by his companions: a meeting across time that remains utterly inconceivable at the level of “opaque and dense time,” the chronological time of our sensory world. Salmân the Pure continues:

“Then the Imam approached the people of 'Âd and called them to faith. They refused. So he went forward to meet them, and they attacked him. We could see them, but they could not see us. Then the Imam withdrew from them and returned to us. He touched our bodies and our hearts with his hand, saying: ‘Remain steadfast in faith.’ Then he went toward them again and once more called them to faith.

“We watched them. Again they refused. Then a single great cry rang out. I swear by the One in whose hand my soul rests! At that moment I thought the earth had turned upside down and the mountains had been flattened. And I saw the people of 'Âd lying on the ground like hollow trunks of palm trees (Quran 69:6–7). Then the Imam said to us: ‘May God never allow your faith to weaken!’” (§ 28).
Reflecting on the paradox of this shared presence within the Malakût, Qâzî Sa'îd writes:

“Understand that there is no contradiction between what happens in our story, which describes how the people of 'Âd perished by the Imam’s sword, and the Quranic account describing how they perished in the violence of an unceasing hurricane. Nor is there any contradiction between the Quranic account of their wrongdoing in centuries past and the battle that the Imam wages against them before the eyes of the companions. For the hurricane, like every host among the divine hosts, obeys the Imam by God’s permission.

“And the Imam himself is the ordeal that strikes his enemies, because he is the Supreme Sign (al-âya al-kubrâ) which they reject. It was through him and by his command that the destruction of earlier generations took place, just as the salvation of the believers among those generations came about through his grace and mercy. For the Imam is present with every prophet, secretly and in a suprasensible way (malakûtan wa sirran: literally, ‘as Malakût’). And it is precisely this companionship within the Malakût that the Imam now allows Salmân the Pure and the other companions to see.”

Thus the teaching of the visionary account reaches its conclusion in what amounts to a direct demonstration, within the Malakût, of a celebrated hadith encountered many times in the course of this work. In it the Prophet declares that “the Imam was sent secretly with every prophet before me, whereas with me he was sent openly.” Because the spiritual reality of the Imam is the inner meaning of the prophetic message, it carries within itself the secret of sacred history—hierohistory—the spiritual, hidden, invisible history of humanity.

Only through the Malakût is authentic contemporaneity established. Those whose individual measures of time have reached the same degree are present together in the same region of the Malakût. And only in the Malakût does the whole become visible, in a way that cannot be compared with the fragmentary vision afforded by the “opaque time” of our historical existence.

Beyond comparison indeed! After one final flight, about which we are told nothing except that the earth now appeared to the companions no longer even the size of a shield, but as small as a little coin—a dirham—the story of the White Cloud ends with a swift return to earth. The companions find themselves once again in the Imam’s house, which they had never physically left, in less than the blink of an eye. The muezzin was chanting the call to the noon prayer.
“And yet,” Salmân the Pure explains, “we had set out at sunrise. Thus we had been to Mount Qâf, traveled around it, and returned within a period of five hours” (§§ 29–30).

These five hours correspond to the five “stations” (maqâmât) that the Imam showed his companions in the Malakût, each station marking one hour. But these five hours are obviously an estimate made according to the outward measurements of our earthly, “opaque and dense” time. There is otherwise no common measure between earthly time and the time of the Malakût, where one can be contemporary with both past and future, and where time becomes space: the space of the soul’s inner distances, which the soul crosses at a speed proportionate to the strength of its longing.

The word “hour” in the Malakût must be understood in the sense it bears in the Quran, where “the Hour” signifies the Day of Resurrection. This is why the reference to “the hour of noon” appears so full of meaning to Qâzî Sa'îd. Noon is the hour when beings cast no shadow; according to certain Iranian traditions, it is always noon in Yima’s Var, his mysterious enclosure. What this hour of noon ultimately announces is the meaning of the story of the White Cloud as an account of initiation.

The companions’ ascent into the Malakût has made them people of the Malakût. That is why, at the beginning, we recalled another mystical ascent: the anagôgê, which for the community that revered the Chaldean Oracles as its sacred book possessed the meaning of a “sacrament of immortality.” Here the companions who have undergone this initiation have passed by the Spring of Life. They have attained the perfectly balanced stature of the spiritual human being. This is what it means to reach the hour of noon, the hour when the muezzin sounds the call to midday prayer.

“That they have reached the hour of noon,” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “indicates that during this journey they have reached the equator of human reality and the equinoctial line of the Imam’s walâyat, for he is the Seal of absolute walâyat.”

And this is why it would be beside the point to subject this visionary hadith, or any similar hadith, to a purely “historical criticism.” What purpose would be served by asking whether this episode occurred in one particular year or another during the Imam’s earthly lifetime? Or whether Salmân was truly the “transmitter” of the account, or whether the text was composed at a later date? Nothing that takes place in it occurs within ordinary chronological history. Its very purpose is to draw us out of that history.

If we treated the text in this way, what would remain in our hands but the torn fragments of a chrysalis? For at what date, in what realm of verifiable historical events, could we place the moment when the Imam truly appeared in this way to a devoted Shiite believer, together with the events that truly followed in the Malakût? We encounter an accomplished reality only where it is actually accomplished. And here its accomplishment does not take place on the stage of visible history. The reality of the hour of noon in the Malakût corresponds to the liturgical time of the muezzin’s call to prayer. Liturgical time is not historical time.

All the elements that make up the spiritual philosophy of the Imams have been contemplated in this way. As in Suhrawardî’s visionary narratives, there comes a privileged instant when a doctrine becomes an event personally experienced in a vision. That is how we come to possess this hadith. Whatever year the person who wrote it down may have taken up his pen, it was indeed Salmân the Pure who told what he had seen—what, to use Semnânî’s language, the “Salmân within his own being” had been capable of seeing.

And if Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî wrote the commentary whose essential meaning we have tried to bring out, it was with an intention he made clear from the very beginning: to lead his reader to take a place upon the White Cloud as well, and rise into the Malakût. Even if the reader cannot fully realize that intention, Qâzî Sa'îd remains one of those Iranian philosophers and spiritual thinkers from whom there is much to learn for anyone who wishes not to “belong to his time” or “keep up with his time,” according to the commonplace slogans of our age, but to be his own time, and to be it completely.

Qâzî Sa'îd’s metaphysics of time is the surest antidote to the illusion of an anonymous, impersonal time supposedly shared by everyone. The fact that several beings coexist within chronological time is not enough to make them contemporaries. The idea that every being possesses its own particular measure, or quantum, of time—which, like its own quantum of substance, passes through different states of density and subtlety—allows us to determine much more surely who our contemporaries are and who they are not.

Contemporaneity, or synchronism, exists when the measure of time belonging to different beings has reached the same state or degree. It means that together they aim toward the same height on the horizon of the Malakût. They can be there together, for example, at the “hour of noon,” and so become contemporaries of the same events, because the measure of time that is truly their own has broken through the irreversible time of History. Entry into the Malakût, and into the time of the Malakût, can only be a mysterium liturgicum, a liturgical mystery. That is what the muezzin’s call to the noon prayer announces to the companions.

At the end of this brief study of Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, a question inevitably arises for the philosophical researcher who has become familiar with a text such as the “Story of the White Cloud” and with the interpretation given to it by a traditional theosopher. The question is this: what impression can this story and its interpretation make on a reader today, when everything in our civilization and culture tends to keep us on this side of Mount Qâf? We can indeed say everything.

For what we call the “human sciences”—sociology and social history, psychology and psychoanalysis—as well as those sciences once called the “divine sciences,” which no longer dare speak their name since a certain theology lost sight of its object along the way: all these disciplines, through the interpretations they impose upon the facts over which they have made themselves judges, tend to close every passage that might allow us to enter Mount Qâf and pass beyond it.

I have sometimes asked myself this question while reflecting on the similarities between the visions described in the “Story of the White Cloud” and certain visions recorded in Swedenborg’s Memorabilia. During one such reflection, I happened to read an article about Strindberg. We know that, at the end of experiences of extraordinary suffering, Strindberg was able to write that Swedenborg had been his guide, the Virgil who enabled him to pass through hell. In that article I found these words quoted:
“From atheism to Swedenborg is only a single step.”

The deeper truth suggested by this brief saying then appeared to me as follows. It is easier to cross Mount Qâf after a devastation that has shattered the Image of himself that Man possessed by virtue of his origin—an origin he knew to be heavenly—than it ever has been, or ever will be, for a comfortable rationalist orthodoxy to make that crossing. Nor does it become any easier when such an orthodoxy is replaced by a theological conformism that throws itself into a frantic pursuit of history, vainly hoping to find salvation in history itself. That race is lost before it begins, even at the cost of the “betrayal of the intellectuals.”

Yet perhaps the metaphysical devastation brought about by our “human sciences” and by a theology in disarray may, on the contrary, make it easier for a few people to rediscover the path to Mount Qâf. What our “human sciences,” no less than a theology concerned solely with outward meanings, have forgotten is that the masters and schools who knew and transmitted the esoteric—that is, the spiritual—meaning of the Bible and the Quran always understood that this spiritual meaning belonged to a transcendent and enduring world. That world remains hidden behind the outward appearance of events that occurred in the “opaque and dense” time of historical chronicles.

Spiritual meaning is not established by reference to a date in chronology, nor as an expression of a social condition. It is the expression of a state of the Malakût. Consequently, whenever scientific facts or discoveries, or new interpretations elevated to the status of established facts, have caused alarm, and people have responded either with apologetic arguments or, as so often today, by trying to outdo the discoveries themselves, the reason has always been the same. They have forgotten that all these facts and discoveries, however immense the expanses of space and time they reveal, remain on this side of Mount Qâf. I believe this symbolic language is particularly appropriate here.

But when there are no longer any “divine sciences,” what can a theology accomplish if it too remains on this side of Mount Qâf? Long before modern scientific discoveries, the vastness of time and space, and the multitude of worlds, had already been revealed to traditional theosophy, as the “Story of the White Cloud” shows us.

But all this presupposed the folding of our time and space back upon themselves. It was revealed as something lying beyond Mount Qâf. That makes all the difference. It would therefore be absurd to confuse traveling from one planet to another by physical means with entering Mount Qâf.

But if a traditional mystical theosophy still exists, it is precisely its task to make use of these discoveries, just as it makes use of any other phenomenon, and turn them into new possible points of entry into the Malakût. I believe Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî and his fellow thinkers would have proceeded in just this way. His metaphysics of being as light seems to call us in precisely this direction. With its own particular variations, this metaphysics belongs to the metaphysics of Light widely professed by the traditional theosophical schools of Christianity and Islam, and by Jewish Kabbalists.

Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî’s doctrine of individual measures, or quanta, of time and space is simply a consequence of an analysis applied to the entire metaphysics of being. Through this analysis, the gulf between what is called Spirit and what is called Matter disappears. There is one and the same Light, differentiated into countless degrees of condensation and subtlety. There is “spiritual matter,” and there is matter in its “material state.” The body, in the world of the Malakût, becomes a subtle spiritual body. Generally speaking, we may say that this traditional metaphysics of Light anticipated many of the results of our modern physics of light, insofar as modern physics has made any rigid boundary between the “material” and the “immaterial” increasingly difficult to maintain.

If I mentioned Strindberg a few lines earlier, it was precisely because Swedenborg’s doctrines revealed to him a metaphysics of Spirit in which spirit is no longer the opposite of body. In this understanding, the idea of body is not limited to the perishable physical body, which is merely its outermost limit. It also embraces a spiritual embodiment, a spiritual corporeality that constitutes the substantial reality of Spirit itself. This idea of spiritual corporeality is essential both to the Platonists of Persia and to all those influenced by the Cambridge Platonists.

And it is here that the work of our Shiite theosopher may be seen to stand in a significant correspondence with another body of thought—one which it might, moreover, help us to clarify. I am thinking of Milton’s doctrines. His Paradise Lost and theological writings show that he had devoted considerable attention to the study of Kabbalah and the Neoplatonists. This example illustrates particularly well the kind of contemporaneity we have been considering. Milton, who died in 1674, and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who died in 1691, were contemporaries in chronological time.

Yet each remained entirely unaware of the other. The dates of the seventeenth century that we can place beside their names are not enough, by themselves, to make them contemporaries in the precise sense in which we are using that word. What makes them contemporaries is the teaching they profess. We might represent their doctrines as two parallel lines, one of which—Milton’s—comes to an end before reaching its full development. Milton professes a doctrine of the Absconditum, the unknowable God of the theology that approaches the divine through negation, similar to that of Shiite theology.

Because he does not accept the Trinitarian theology of the Council of Nicaea, Milton regards the Logos, the “Son,” not as a principle coeternal with the “Father,” but as the Deus revelatus: the God who is brought into being and manifested, at once the creator of the world and the substance of his creation. He sees in Christ a second creation, who is both creator and substance of the Elect. His doctrine of the Holy Spirit recalls the uncertainties of pre-Nicene Christology concerning the two figures of the Son and the Spirit, and it has certain affinities with the ways in which the Holy Spirit is understood in Islamic theosophy. To the extent that Shiite Imamology and Quranic Christology correspond to the form of Christology associated with Arius, we could draw a parallel here with the theosophical doctrine of the Muhammadan Light, or Muhammadan Logos, and the Imam’s role in salvation.

Although philosophical anthropology would have much to learn from it, no comparative synthesis of this kind has ever been attempted. It seems that such an undertaking could bear fruit only if it developed within a horizon that was no longer “Christian” in the historical sense of the word, but Christic: centered on the spiritual reality of Christ. That, however, is not the aspect on which I intend to concentrate as I draw this study to a close. The point I want to bring into focus is Milton’s conception of matter. This conception is fairly well known. It has sometimes been called a Christian materialism.

But it would be just as accurate to call it an absolute spiritualism. For Milton’s idea of matter, which he shares with the Kabbalists and Neoplatonists he had read, is also the idea we find in a Shiite theosopher such as Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. It is the idea of a universal first matter, a materia prima universalis, common to everything we call spirit and everything we call body: a universal matter passing through every degree of subtlety and density.

Thus there is no longer an essential difference between spirit and body. There is a difference of degree. But a continuous range of degrees requires an intermediate realm. And that is precisely what the Illuminationist (ishrâqî) and Shiite traditions designate as the mundus imaginalis of the Malakût:
“the world in which bodies become spiritual and spirits take on bodily form.”

Perhaps, then, what Milton lacked, to a greater or lesser extent, was a rigorous account of the reality and structure of this Malakût—an understanding that Islamic theosophy had possessed since Suhrawardî. For the completion of the whole Image of the human being after death cannot take place without the light of the Malakût. Given his starting principles, Milton cannot conceive of the human being simply as a combination of what scholastic philosophy called soul and body.

Still less can he understand death as the separation of soul and body, leaving a formless, shapeless soul to exist on its own while waiting to be reunited with its resurrected body. Such fragile conceptions are capable of bringing an entire system down in their eventual collapse. For Milton, the immortality of the soul without the immortality of the body makes no sense. Certainly, since all things have come forth from God (fuisse omnia ex Deo), nothing can perish, and in that sense death does not exist.
